people.question: Who is Richard Guise?

accounts.title: The French account
accounts.source: Family tradition, and the Bell family database
accounts.summary: A Frenchman from Lorraine who fled the Revolution, took the King's shilling in England, and was sent to the other side of the world.
points: 14 October 1789 — joined the Royal Grenadier Horse Guards in England.
1792 — landed at Sydney aboard the Atlantic, a corporal in the 102nd Regiment: the New South Wales Corps, the Rum Corps.
Died 16 April 1821 at Liverpool, NSW, aged 64, of a liver complaint.
accounts.caveat: The family chart gives his death as 9-4-1821 — a week out from the database.

accounts.title: The English account
accounts.source: Researcher Gillian D.R., and the Guise baronets of Gloucestershire
accounts.summary: An old English gentry name from Gloucestershire, reached by way of Richard Guise of Clewer, Berkshire.
points: Points to the Guise baronets of Elmore and Highnam, Gloucestershire.
Richard Guise of Clewer: Cambridge BMus 1758; lay vicar at St George's Chapel Windsor and at Eton.
Later choirmaster at Westminster Abbey and a Gentleman of the Chapel Royal.
Married Elizabeth Windham, December 1761, at St George's Hanover Square.
accounts.caveat: Read this one carefully: the Clewer Richard is a DIFFERENT MAN. He never came to New South Wales, and he was buried fifteen years before ours died. What this line offers is a possible wider family, not an identity.

accounts.title: They may not be opposed
accounts.source: A reading that reconciles the two
accounts.summary: Both can be true at different depths of the same tree.
points: Guise is a town in Picardy, northern France.
The Gloucestershire Guises are themselves a Norman family — de Guise.
They came to England centuries before either man was born.
So an English surname with a French origin is not a contradiction. It is the usual story.

people.wouldSettleIt: His enlistment or discharge papers for the 102nd Regiment, or a baptism record tying a Richard Guise born about 1757 to either country. Until one of those turns up, this record holds both accounts and asserts neither. He was not on the First Fleet either way — the Atlantic brought him out in 1792, four years after it.
